A coding agent is an AI assistant that works inside your project rather than in
a chat window. It reads your files, runs R and Quarto, changes code and text,
and checks the result, for instance by rendering a report and reading the
errors. Paired with Git and GitHub, every change it makes is recorded, and you
can read it, discuss it, undo it or keep it.

This page describes how I work this way on this website, my teaching materials
and research code, and how to set it up for a project like the one in [R and
Quarto: a short start](r-quarto.qmd).

## What you need {#need}

- **A GitHub repository for your project.** A repository is a project folder
  under version control: Git records every change with a message, and GitHub
  keeps a copy online where you can browse it, compare versions and review
  changes. Private repositories are free. If Git is new to you, [Happy Git and
  GitHub for the useR](https://happygitwithr.com/) explains the one-time setup,
  and from an RStudio project `usethis::use_git()` and
  [`usethis::use_github()`](https://usethis.r-lib.org/reference/use_github.html)
  do the rest.
- **A coding agent.** I use [Claude
  Code](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/overview), from Anthropic. It runs in a
  terminal, in VS Code and JetBrains editors, in a desktop app, and in the
  browser at [claude.ai/code](https://claude.ai/code), where each session runs
  in the cloud on a copy of your repository. OpenAI's
  [Codex](https://developers.openai.com/codex) and GitHub's [Copilot coding
  agent](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/agents/coding-agent/about-coding-agent)
  work along the same lines. These tools generally need a paid plan.

In the browser, the agent works in a cloud environment of its own and installs
what it needs there, and your computer can be off. On your computer, it uses
what you have installed. Either way, what the agent reads is sent to its
provider, which matters for your data (see [what stays with
you](#judgement)).

## The workflow {#workflow}

1. **Describe the project once,** in a short file in the repository's main
   folder that the agent reads at the start of every session (see [the next
   section](#instructions)).
2. **Give one task per session,** in plain words: the goal, who it is for, and
   what *done* looks like.
3. **Let the agent work on a branch.** It makes its changes on a separate
   branch, renders and checks them, commits them with messages that say why,
   and pushes the branch to GitHub. Your main branch stays as it was.
4. **Review.** Read the changes on GitHub, where a pull request shows every
   changed line; render the branch yourself; ask questions or for changes in
   the same session.
5. **Merge** the branch into main when you are satisfied, and publish if the
   project is a report or a website.
6. **Update the instructions.** When the agent gets something wrong twice, add
   a line to them, so the next session starts knowing it.

This page was written that way: in a cloud session with my website's
repository, on its own branch, and reviewed by me before it was merged.

## A file of instructions {#instructions}

Claude Code reads a file called `CLAUDE.md`; Codex, Copilot and most other
agents read `AGENTS.md`, a [shared format](https://agents.md/). Keep it short
and concrete: how to build and check the project, its conventions, and what to
ask about first. For a thesis in R and Quarto it could start like this:

```{.markdown filename="CLAUDE.md"}
# Project notes

Master's thesis on [topic]. Text in Quarto (.qmd files), analysis in R.

## Build and check
- `quarto render` builds the thesis as PDF and web version into _book/.
- Render after every change; fix all errors and warnings before committing.
- `Rscript R/01_clean.R` rebuilds the clean data from data/raw/.

## Conventions
- Paths relative to the project folder; never setwd().
- tidyverse style with the |> pipe; one numbered script per step in R/.
- No numbers typed into the text: use inline R.
- British English, short sentences.

## Data
- data/raw/ holds the original files: never change them, never commit them
  (they are listed in .gitignore).
- Never print individual records.

## Ask before
- changing the sample, a variable definition or a model;
- deleting files or rewriting Git history.
```

In Claude Code, the `/init` command drafts such a file from your repository;
shorten the draft and add your own rules. Rules about the statistics belong
here too. The instructions in the repository of my journal club talk, for
example, say: "report both models and the fixed validation split. Do not select
a model or split because it yields a stronger signal"
([`AGENTS.md`](https://github.com/valentinklotzbuecher/jcod/blob/main/AGENTS.md)).

To serve several agents from one file, write `AGENTS.md` and start `CLAUDE.md`
with the line `@AGENTS.md`, which imports it ([more](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory)).

## Prompts that work {#prompts}

Write as you would to a capable research assistant who has not seen the
project: the goal, the context, and how you will judge the result. Ask for a
check at the end and for a short note on anything left undone. For example:

- *Turn `analysis.R` into a Quarto report, `report.qmd`, that renders to HTML
  and Word. Hide the code in the output, put the numbers in the text with
  inline R, and cross-reference the figures. Render both formats and fix any
  errors.*
- *Add a Table 1 by treatment group with gtsummary and refer to it in the
  results section.*
- *Set up my thesis from the template in the GitHub repository
  valentinklotzbuecher/ufr_thesis, with my name and title and three empty
  chapters: Introduction, Data, Results.*
- *Review `R/03_models.R` for mistakes such as wrong variables, silently
  dropped missing values or factor coding. Don't change anything; list what you
  find with line numbers.*
- *Explain what `R/02_merge.R` does, step by step, for someone new to dplyr.*

For a larger change, ask for a plan first and agree on it before any code is
written. Keep tasks small: a session that does one thing is easier to review
than one that does five.

## What stays with you {#judgement}

- **The decisions.** The research question, the analysis plan, the sample, the
  model and what the results mean. An agent will propose answers to all of
  them; they are yours to make and to defend.
- **The checking.** Read every change before you merge it, and rerun the
  analysis yourself. Agents are fast and sound sure of themselves when they are
  wrong: they misread a variable, or make a failing check pass by loosening it.
- **The data.** Keep identifiable personal data, such as patient data, out of
  the repository and out of the agent's reach, and follow your institution's
  rules. A line in `CLAUDE.md` is a request, not a lock. Where the real data
  cannot be shared, the agent can write and test the code on synthetic data
  with the same structure, and you run it on the real data yourself.
- **The rules on AI use.** Universities, journals and employers have them.
  Check what applies, and say how you used AI: in a thesis, usually in the
  declaration of independent work.

In a study I co-authored, [AI-assisted teams assessed the reproducibility of
published research better than AI-led teams, but not better than human-only
teams](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2524747123).

## Going further {#reading}

- Claude Code: [overview](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/overview), [working in
